slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; it should put the cash into its software and reopen quick commerce only if customer sites prove it pays
Quick commerce is growing fast, but no operator has yet made it profitable
–	US sales grew 2.8 times in three years, to $5.1B in 2025
–	Both incumbents lose money per order; QuickBasket closed 4 of 11 cities
At the economics of Parcelbird's own customer sites every order loses money, and pricing does not close the gap
–	At the median customer site, each order would lose $6.17
–	Even best-on-every-driver loses about $1.80 an order; the plan assumes more
The plan breaks the 12-month runway floor even on the founders' own numbers
–	Spending $9.5M to month 18 leaves about 6 months of runway
–	At median economics nine stores would lose about $18M a year
Scaling the software is the better use of cash; reopen quick commerce only when gates are met
–	Software hires use 11% of cash above the floor; the launch needs 132%
–	Nine late-stage deals would add about $0.9M of ARR, above the $0.8M hires' cost

Resetting either basket size or rider speed alone to the median turns the plan's profit into a loss
Founders' plan contribution per order after store costs, one driver reset to the benchmark median, $ per order
Two of the four drivers each carry the whole profit
▪	Basket size: the plan's $45 is 32% above the median, and no site has reached it
▪	Rider speed: the plan needs riders 46% faster than the median, above any site's pace
▪	Volume and promotions: either one alone leaves the plan barely above zero
▪	Both at the median: the plan would lose about $3.06 an order, half the median site's loss
1  Each bar changes one driver of the founders' plan to the benchmark median and keeps the others at plan values
